title: Primitive streak

objective.text: Describe the primitive streak: where it forms, its parts and how long it lasts.

body.general: Where does gastrulation begin? Around day 15 a groove, the primitive streak, forms in the midline at the tail end of the disc [f1]. Its head end swells into a small knot, the primitive node, around a dip called the primitive pit [f2]. The streak marks the long axis: the head end is the opposite end [f3]. It keeps feeding cells inward until the end of week 4, then shrinks and disappears [f4].
body.mbbs: The primitive streak first appears as a faint line in the caudal midline of the epiblast [f1]. By days 15–16 it is a narrow groove with raised edges [f1]. At its cranial end sits the primitive node, a low mound with the primitive pit at its centre [f2]. The streak defines the cranial–caudal axis: it lies caudally, and the cranial end is opposite [f3]. It keeps making cells until the end of week 4, then regresses quickly and disappears [f4].

facts.text: The streak first shows as a faint line in the caudal midline; by days 15–16 it is a narrow groove with raised edges.
facts.note: R06: streak at ~13 d post-ovulation, within the ±1–2 d spread (dossier §1)

facts.text: Its cranial end is the primitive node, a low mound with the primitive pit at its centre.
It marks the body's long axis: the head end is opposite the streak, which lies caudally.
It keeps adding cells until the end of week 4, then shrinks fast and disappears.
facts.note: R05a: gastrulation area still present caudally to ~CS10 — consistent, not a direct confirmation

facts.text: Leftover streak cells in the sacrococcygeal region can form a sacrococcygeal teratoma.
It is the most common tumour in newborns.
This tumour holds tissue from all three germ layers and is often found on scans before birth.

misconceptions.wrong: The primitive streak is permanent and becomes the spine.
misconceptions.right: It shrinks and disappears after week 4; leftovers can form a sacrococcygeal teratoma.

misconceptions.wrong: The primitive streak is the notochord.
misconceptions.right: The streak is where cells move in; the notochord is a rod built later from some of those cells.

checks.prompt: What happens to the primitive streak after week 4?
checks.why: The streak regresses fast after week 4 and leaves no adult structure.

options: At the cranial end of the streak
At the caudal end of the streak
At the rim of the disc
checks.why: The node is the raised area at the streak's cranial end, around the primitive pit.

checks.prompt: Which best describes the primitive streak?
options: The groove where epiblast cells move in
The rod that signals the spine to form
The first part of the spinal cord
checks.why: The streak is a groove of moving cells; the notochord is a separate rod made later.

adult: The streak leaves no adult part; what lasts is the head-to-tail axis it marked [f3,f4].

remember.q: Where does the primitive streak form?
remember.a: In the caudal midline of the disc, as a groove by days 15–16 [f1].

remember.q: What lies at the cranial end of the streak?
remember.a: The primitive node, around the primitive pit [f2].
After the end of week 4, when it shrinks fast [f4].

clinical: If streak cells survive near the tailbone (the sacrococcygeal region), they can form a tumour called a sacrococcygeal teratoma [f5]. It holds tissue from all three germ layers [f7]. It is the most common tumour in newborns [f6].
